absent: Full structure definitions with field order, sizes and alignment for domain, group, capacity, shared, root, deadline heap and priority tracker are not present in these fragments.
Locking discipline for group acquisition, capacity updates and domain construction beyond mutex assertions and lock initialization is not shown.
Runtime consumption of balance masks, capacity values and asymmetric preference ordering during load balancing is not defined here.
Clock, tick, NUMA distance table and node reclaim threshold inputs referenced during tuning are not defined in these fragments.
Performance domain structure, capacity span storage and SMT neighborhood derivation are not shown.
Concurrent teardown ordering and live object lifetime beyond staged release and reference transfer are not specified.
Architecture override conditions for topology refresh and consumer contracts for domain mask arrays are not specified.

findings.text: Deadline ordered CPU tracking provides externally visible creation and teardown that manage element storage and idle membership lifecycle with resource exhaustion reported on failure.
Priority ordered CPU tracking provides externally visible creation and teardown that manage per priority membership and per CPU current priority storage with partial release on failure.

Deadline bandwidth management provides externally visible initialization that derives allowance from global real time controls and clears accumulated usage, with global runtime helper translating control settings into nanosecond units or unlimited indication.
Scheduler domain mask array management provides externally visible allocation that provisions each entry with rollback of earlier entries on failure, plus symmetric release of entries and container.
Scheduler address classification provides an externally visible query that identifies addresses belonging to scheduler implementation or locking implementation ranges.
Top level task grouping object is globally visible as the ancestor for all scheduling entities.

Group acquisition reuses shared descriptors through reference counting so repeated visits obtain the same initialized object while the initial visit establishes span membership and capacity state derived from child domain or single CPU.

Group capacity preparation derives membership weight and distinct core estimates from span topology and records asymmetric preference only when packing behavior is enabled, refreshing shared capacity when invoked on the designated balancer.

Domain initialization derives membership from allowed CPUs intersected with level membership and establishes balancing intervals, success accounting, timestamps and default behaviors augmented by architecture and asymmetry inputs, with later refinement for sharing, cache locality and NUMA distance characteristics.

Domain construction links child and parent with increasing level tracking and enforces containment of child membership within parent with corrective enlargement and diagnostics on violation, then resolves relax thresholds from request or default to suppress selected balancing behaviors on deep domains.
Asymmetry detection counts distinct capacity spans intersecting the domain versus those present only in the overall map to distinguish absence, partial and complete asymmetry indications.
Topology validation requires non NUMA levels to be pairwise identical or disjoint as identified by lowest member, explicitly skipping NUMA levels that may overlap to protect group linkage.
NUMA imbalance allowance is derived from last level cache grouping density and propagated upward scaled by relative span sizes starting from the first NUMA ancestor.

Shared descriptor assignment scans domain membership for an unclaimed or flag compatible slot with tolerance for single member domains and fallback reuse with diagnostic on exhaustion, while asymmetric claiming locates the nearest fully asymmetric non NUMA ancestor before requesting shared state for it.

Topology storage creation provisions per level per CPU domain, group and capacity objects with node locality, self linked group lists and per CPU identifiers, plus per CPU shared descriptors, reporting exhaustion on any allocation shortfall.

Ownership claiming detaches live objects from temporary tables by clearing entries whose reference counts indicate use while walking domain ancestry, and staged release disposes only acquired levels in reverse order including special NUMA group handling and pointer clearing.

Root domain lifecycle zero allocates the container then initializes masks, bandwidth, deadline and priority tracking with ordered rollback on failure, while teardown via deferred reclamation releases trackers, masks, performance list and container, with performance release having an active walk variant and an empty variant for configurations without that feature.
Last level cache identifier management allocates the lowest free value under protection, tracks the observed maximum and reports exhaustion when beyond the possible CPU limit.
Task group slab cache pointer is constrained to remain immutable after initialization completes.
Span validation and cache identifier allocation each require the scheduler domains mutex to be held by the caller.
Deadline tracking, deadline bandwidth and real time push state each own a spin based lock initialized during creation for later synchronized access.

Root domain aggregates deadline and priority trackers plus span and online membership, overload and push masks, performance list, bandwidth state, visit generation and deferred reclamation linkage with reference count governing release.

Scheduling group couples span and balance membership with flags, weight, core count and asymmetric preference, linked circularly and associated to a shared capacity object holding reference counts and capacity bounds, while scheduling domain links child and parent plus sibling groups, shared accounting and private level storage with level, flags, name, span weight and balancing tuning.

Topology level descriptor provides a membership callback with optional flag callback, name, NUMA depth and per level storage tables iterated until a terminator, while shared accounting holds allocation flags with busy and reference counts and deadline plus priority trackers pair slot indices with per priority counts, masks and per CPU values.
Domain allocation advances through storage, shared, domain array and root stages with a completion marker that drives reverse ordered release of only the stages actually acquired.
Root initialization acquires span, online and overload masks then bandwidth, deadline and priority state, unwinding in reverse order to the failure point and signaling resource exhaustion.
Early boot entry starts scheduling on the boot processor and reports success.
Architecture topology refresh provides a weak default that reports success when no platform override exists.

Reference skew between group and capacity visits, unsupported flag combinations and simultaneous sharing plus asymmetry indications each trigger warnings with flag masking to safe subsets, while missing shared descriptors trigger a one time warning with reuse of the last examined entry.
Malformed topology with non subset child spans logs diagnostics and repairs by union enlargement, while inconsistent non NUMA spans that partially overlap cause validation failure.
Exhaustion of memory during any provisioning step or of cache identifiers beyond possible CPUs is signaled as a failure code with prior partial allocations released in reverse order.

Group capacity accounting is expressed in units of a scheduler capacity scale with initial current, minimum and maximum bounds derived from span size, while deadline heap and priority tracking each define a distinguished invalid marker for empty slots with a fixed count of priority levels.

Global real time allowance treats a negative control as unlimited and otherwise scales a microsecond control into nanoseconds for bandwidth derivation, while balancing behavior starts from defined interval, factor, tolerance and idle success ratio defaults later refined by sharing class.
